De Stijl

The Dutch movement around the journal De Stijl (1917–1931) and Mondrian’s neoplasticism: compositions built only from horizontal and vertical lines and rectangular planes, in the three primary colors and the three non-colors black, white, and gray, balanced by asymmetry instead of symmetry.

Orthogonal / Balanced / Austere / Pure

Visual grammar

  • Only horizontals and verticals. Straight black lines of equal or varied weight divide the surface into rectangles. There are no curves and, in the core style, no diagonals.
  • Primaries and non-colors. Red, yellow, and blue as flat, unmixed planes, with black, white, and gray. Mondrian’s paintings of 1920–1921 use several whites and grays and some solid black planes. White and gray usually cover most of the surface.
  • Asymmetric balance. Planes of unequal size balance by opposition: a large colored plane against small ones in the far corners. Lines run to the edge of the field or stop just short of it.
  • Flat planes. No modelling, texture, shadow, or gradient. In furniture and buildings, planes and bars overlap without joining, each one painted in its own color.
  • Rectilinear capitals. Blocky sans-serif letters built from straight strokes, as in van Doesburg’s 1919 alphabet. Capitals and letter-spaced titles are common.
  • No images of things. Pure abstraction. Nothing is depicted. Color and proportion carry the whole composition.

What connects the references

Mondrian’s paintings of 1920–1921 set the core grammar: a white center ringed by black, gray, and primary planes, or one large blue plane answered by small red, black, and yellow ones. The primaries in both are less pure than later pastiche, and gray and black cover as much area as color.

Van Doesburg shows the range of the movement. His Composition XXII drops the black lines and uses ochre and gray-green; his 1917 windows are dense mirrored patterns with green and brown glass; the Aubette ciné-dancing turns the grid 45°, which is Elementarism. The black line grid is Mondrian’s signature more than a rule of the whole group.

Type and print follow the same rule: van Doesburg’s alphabet and Section d’Or poster design build letters from right angles only, and the journal cover and advertisements use black capitals, one red, vertical text, and thick black bars as frames.

In three dimensions the planes separate: the Schröder House and the Red Blue Chair use primaries as thin bars or single boards against white, gray, and black, and Café De Unie makes a facade into a graphic panel with lettering.

Websites in the style are rare. Of about 25 candidates checked on 28 September 2026, one is a clear example, a small student page on Neocities whose header is a Mondrian grid. Four are borderline: the Van Doesburghuis uses flat primary panels without black lines, the Mondriaanhuis uses offset line frames and yellow, Mondrian Generator draws compositions as images beside square outlined controls, and the 100 jaar De Stijl holding page has only a rectilinear logo. No kept site passes the fingerprint.

The fingerprint is therefore not calibrated on real sites. The main blind spot is the line: web imitations draw black bars as filled boxes or grid gaps, so surface.border.medianWidth reads 1 px, and generators draw the composition in a canvas that computed styles cannot see. Judge such pages by the rubric.

Neoplasticism, Neo-plasticism, Nieuwe Beelding, The Style
Era
1917–1931. From the first issue of the journal to Theo van Doesburg’s death. The look continues in later revivals, often as a “Mondrian” pattern.

Lineage

  • Influenced by Cubism. Wikidata (P737) and Wikipedia name Cubist painting as an influence. Mondrian’s grids of about 1914–1916 grew out of Cubist work in Paris.
  • Related to Neoplasticism. Mondrian’s theory, first named in the journal in 1917. Tate treats it as the name for the art that the De Stijl circle practised, so this record uses it as an alias for the core of the style.
  • Related to Elementarism. Van Doesburg’s later branch (from about 1924) that admits diagonals. Tate and Wikipedia record that Mondrian left the group over it. This record covers the orthogonal core and treats diagonal work as this branch.
  • Related to Bauhaus. Van Doesburg taught informal De Stijl courses in Weimar in 1921–1922, and Wikipedia states that De Stijl influenced the Bauhaus style.
  • Related to Constructivism. Wikidata (P737) and Wikipedia record that Malevich and Russian Constructivism influenced the group after about 1921.

Classification rubric

The test for a new reference

Identifies the style

  • Every line and edge is horizontal or vertical.
  • Thick black lines divide the surface into rectangles.
  • Flat red, yellow, and blue planes sit among larger white or gray planes.
  • The composition is asymmetric but balanced.

Rules it out

  • Circles, curves, or rounded corners.
  • Diagonals as the main structure (that is Elementarism or Constructivism).
  • Secondary or pastel colors such as green, orange, purple, or pink.
  • Gradients, shadows, textures, or photographs.

Often confused with

Bauhaus
Bauhaus uses circles, triangles, and diagonals and often lowercase type. De Stijl uses only rectangles and straight horizontal and vertical lines.
International Typographic Style
The Swiss style uses the grid invisibly and relies on type, often with one accent color. De Stijl makes the grid visible as thick black lines and fills cells with primary colors.
Neo-brutalism
Neo-brutalism also uses thick black outlines and bright fills, but adds hard offset shadows, rounded corners, and pastel or secondary colors.
Constructivism
Constructivism is built on diagonals, red and black, and photomontage. De Stijl is orthogonal and does not use images.
Memphis
Memphis clashes many colors, patterns, and irregular shapes. De Stijl keeps three primaries and three non-colors in plain rectangles.

Ideas to carry forward

  • Build the layout as a visible grid: thick black lines between rectangular cells.
  • Use flat red, yellow, and blue for a few cells. Keep most cells white or light gray.
  • Make the balance asymmetric: one large colored plane, and smaller ones in the opposite corners.
  • Use a condensed or square sans-serif in capitals for headings.
  • Let lines run through to the edge of the container.

Keep the function

  • Do not use rounded corners, circles, or curved shapes.
  • Do not use diagonals, rotation, or skew.
  • Do not use green, orange, purple, or tints of the primaries.
  • Do not use gradients, shadows, textures, or photographs.

Useful directions: museums and exhibitions, architecture and furniture studios, design education, posters and event sites.

Poor fits:

  • Content-heavy sites and apps. The grid of colored planes leaves little room for text.
  • Warm, organic, or caring brands.
